**Short answer** | What you need to do | UK GDPR (post‑Brexit) | EU GDPR (Germany) | |---------------------|-----------------------|-------------------| | **Legal basis for the transfer** | *Adequacy decision* (none for Germany yet) **or** “appropriate safeguards” – e.g. UK Standard Contractual Clauses (UK‑SCCs), Binding Corporate Rules, or a DPIA that shows the level of protection is equivalent to an adequacy decision. | Same: either an EU adequacy decision (Germany is in‑EU so no need) **or** “appropriate safeguards” – EU SCCs, BCRs, or a DPIA that demonstrates equivalence. | | **Special‑category data?** | If HR records contain health, biometric, racial/ethnic origin, etc., they are *special categories* under the UK DPA 2018 and require explicit consent or another specific lawful basis (e.g., Article 6(1)(b) for employment purposes). | Same – special‑category data requires explicit consent or a specific lawful basis (Article 6(1)(b) or (f)). | | **Processor agreement** | Must contain the same clauses as an EU processor contract plus UK‑specific additions: 1) reference to the UK DPA 2018, 2) right of the controller to audit, 3) obligation to notify the regulator of any breach. | Standard EU processor contract (Art 28 GDPR) – no extra UK clauses needed. | | **Documentation you must keep** | • Transfer Impact Assessment / DPIA (if high‑risk).
• Copy of the UK SCCs or BCRs, plus evidence that they are supplemented with adequate safeguards.
• Record of employee consent (if used).
• Records of processing activities (Art 30 GDPR + Art 30 UK DPA 2018). | • Transfer Impact Assessment / DPIA (if high‑risk).
• Copy of the EU SCCs or BCRs, plus evidence that they are supplemented with adequate safeguards.
• Record of employee consent (if used).
• Records of processing activities (Art 30 GDPR). | | **Enforcement position** | • UK regulators have been tightening scrutiny on “supplementary safeguards” after *Schrems II*.
• The UK Data Protection Act 2018 requires that any transfer to a third country be protected by an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards.
• Recent case law (e.g., *Parker v. UK* and the “UK‑SCCs” guidance) stresses that the UK must ensure the level of protection is equivalent to an EU adequacy decision. | • The European Court of Justice (ECJ) has ruled that SCCs are valid only if supplemented with adequate safeguards when the destination country does not have an adequacy decision.
• German supervisory authority (BfDI) requires that any transfer be justified by a DPIA or other evidence of equivalence. | --- ## 1. What each regime requires ### 1.1 UK GDPR & Data Protection Act 2018 | Requirement | Detail | |-------------|--------| | **Legal basis for the transfer** | The UK DPA 2018 (Art 45) says a transfer outside the UK is lawful only if:
• an adequacy decision exists, **or**
• “appropriate safeguards” are in place.
UK has its own adequacy decisions (e.g., EU, Switzerland). Germany is not on that list yet, so you must rely on appropriate safeguards. | | **Appropriate safeguards** | • UK Standard Contractual Clauses (UK‑SCCs) – the UK version of the EU SCCs, approved by the UK Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO).
• Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) if you have a multinational group structure.
• A DPIA that demonstrates the level of protection is equivalent to an adequacy decision. | | **Special‑category data** | If HR records contain health, biometric, racial/ethnic origin, etc., they are “special categories” under the UK DPA 2018 (Art 9). Processing such data requires explicit consent or a specific lawful basis (e.g., Article 6(1)(b) – employment purposes). | | **Processor agreement** | Must contain all clauses of an EU processor contract plus:
• Reference to the UK DPA 2018.
• Right of audit by the controller.
• Obligation to notify ICO of any breach within 72 h. | | **Documentation & record‑keeping** | • Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) or DPIA if high‑risk.
• Copy of UK SCCs/BCRs and evidence that they are supplemented with adequate safeguards.
• Records of processing activities (Art 30 GDPR + Art 30 UK DPA).
• Evidence of employee consent where used. | | **Enforcement** | • ICO has been actively enforcing the “supplementary safeguards” requirement after *Schrems II*.
• The ICO’s guidance on UK SCCs (2023) stresses that you must demonstrate equivalence to an EU adequacy decision, not just rely on the SCC text. | ### 1.2 EU GDPR & German Law | Requirement | Detail | |-------------|--------| | **Legal basis for the transfer** | Art 45 GDPR: Transfer is lawful if there is an adequacy decision by the European Commission or “appropriate safeguards” are in place. Germany is part of the EU, so no adequacy decision is needed – you must use appropriate safeguards. | | **Appropriate safeguards** | • EU Standard Contractual Clauses (EU‑SCCs) approved by the European Commission.
• Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs).
• DPIA that shows equivalence to an adequacy decision. | | **Special‑category data** | Same as UK – special categories require explicit consent or a specific lawful basis (Art 6(1)(b) for employment purposes, Art 9(2)(f) for public interest in the workplace). | | **Processor agreement** | Must comply with Art 28 GDPR: confidentiality, security, sub‑processing, data subject rights, audit rights. No extra UK clauses needed. | | **Documentation & record‑keeping** | • DPIA if high‑risk (Art 35).
• Copy of EU SCCs/BCRs and evidence of supplementary safeguards.
• Records of processing activities (Art 30).
• Evidence of employee consent where used. | | **Enforcement** | • ECJ ruling in *Schrems II* (2020) requires that SCCs be supplemented with adequate safeguards when the destination country does not have an adequacy decision.
• German supervisory authority (BfDI) enforces this rigorously; a DPIA or other evidence of equivalence is mandatory for high‑risk transfers. | --- ## 2. Where the two regimes diverge | Divergence | UK GDPR | EU GDPR | |------------|---------|---------| | **Adequacy decisions** | The UK has its own list (e.g., EU, Switzerland). Germany is *not* on that list yet, so you cannot rely on an adequacy decision. | Germany is in‑EU; no adequacy decision needed for intra‑EU transfers. | | **Standard Contractual Clauses** | UK SCCs are a separate set approved by the ICO. They must be supplemented with additional safeguards to meet the “equivalence” requirement after *Schrems II*. | EU SCCs are approved by the European Commission and can be used directly, but still require supplementary safeguards if the destination country lacks an adequacy decision (which is not the case here). | | **Special‑category data** | UK DPA 2018 has a slightly broader definition of “special categories” (e.g., includes biometric data for identification purposes). | EU GDPR’s definition is narrower; however, both require explicit consent or specific lawful basis. | | **Employment‑specific lawful basis** | Article 6(1)(b) – “processing necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party” – is explicitly recognized as a lawful basis for employment data in UK law. | Same article applies, but the EU has an additional public‑interest clause (Art 6(1)(e)) that can be used for employee data if it is “necessary in the public interest.” | | **Enforcement emphasis** | ICO’s guidance on *supplementary safeguards* after *Schrems II* is very explicit; failure to demonstrate equivalence can lead to fines. | BfDI and other EU supervisory authorities enforce the ECJ ruling; a DPIA or equivalent evidence of adequacy is mandatory for high‑risk transfers. | --- ## 3. Documentation you should prepare | Document | Why it matters | Where it sits in the legal framework | |----------|----------------|-------------------------------------| | **Transfer Impact Assessment / DPIA** | Demonstrates that the transfer is not “high risk” or, if it is, shows how risks are mitigated. Required under Art 35 GDPR (EU) and Art 45(2)(b) UK DPA 2018 for high‑risk transfers. | Must be kept in your records of processing activities (Art 30). | | **UK Standard Contractual Clauses** (or EU SCCs if you choose to use them under the “adequate” approach) | Provides the contractual basis that satisfies Art 45(2)(b) UK DPA 2018 and Art 46 GDPR. | Attach as Annex A to your processor agreement; keep a copy in your records of processing activities. | | **Evidence of supplementary safeguards** (e.g., technical measures, data‑minimisation procedures, encryption, audit logs) | Required by the ICO after *Schrems II* and by the ECJ for SCCs when adequacy is not granted. | Include a summary in your DPIA or as an addendum to the SCCs. | | **Processor Agreement** (updated with UK‑specific clauses if using UK SCCs) | Art 28 GDPR / Art 45(2)(b) UK DPA 2018 require that the processor’s obligations are clearly defined. | Signed and stored in your records of processing activities. | | **Record of employee consent** (if you rely on consent as a lawful basis) | Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous (Art 7 GDPR / Art 9(2)(a) UK DPA). | Store the signed consents or electronic records; include them in your DPIA if relevant. | | **Records of processing activities** (Art 30 GDPR + Art 30 UK DPA 2018) | Must list all transfers, legal bases, categories of data, recipients, and safeguards. | Keep a master spreadsheet or database that is updated whenever the transfer changes. | | **Data Subject Rights Procedure** | Employees must be able to exercise their rights (access, rectification, erasure, objection). | Document how you will respond to requests; include it in your DPIA and processor agreement. | --- ## 4. Practical steps for the company 1. **Choose the safeguards** *If you already have UK SCCs in place*: keep them but add a “supplementary safeguard” clause that lists all technical and organisational measures (encryption, access controls, audit logs). *If you prefer EU SCCs*: they can be used directly for an intra‑EU transfer, but you still need to document that the level of protection is equivalent to an adequacy decision. 2. **Update the processor agreement** Add UK‑specific clauses if using UK SCCs: reference to the UK DPA 2018, audit rights, breach notification to ICO, and a clause that the processor will not process for other purposes. 3. **Conduct a DPIA** (or TIA) *High‑risk* because you are transferring employee data across borders. The DPIA should cover: risk assessment, mitigation measures, legal basis, and evidence of equivalence. 4. **Document supplementary safeguards** Provide a technical specification sheet that shows encryption standards (AES‑256), key management, access logs, incident response procedures, etc. 5. **Keep records** Store all documents in your central data protection repository; ensure they are accessible to the ICO and German supervisory authority if requested. 6. **Train staff** Ensure HR personnel understand that employee data is being transferred abroad and that they must follow the new procedures for data subject rights and breach notification. --- ## 5. Enforcement snapshot (as of August 2026) | Authority | Key enforcement stance | |-----------|------------------------| | **UK ICO** | Actively audits companies using UK SCCs; requires evidence of equivalence after *Schrems II*. Fines up to £17.5 m or 4 % of global turnover for non‑compliance. | | **German BfDI (and other EU supervisory authorities)** | Enforces the ECJ ruling that SCCs must be supplemented with adequate safeguards; requires a DPIA for high‑risk transfers. Fines up to €20 m or 4 % of annual worldwide turnover. | | **European Data Protection Board (EDPB)** | Continues to issue guidelines on “supplementary safeguards” and the use of SCCs post‑*Schrems II*. | --- ### Bottom line - **UK**: No adequacy decision for Germany → rely on UK SCCs + supplementary safeguards. - **EU**: Intra‑EU transfer → EU SCCs are fine, but you still need a DPIA or evidence of equivalence if the transfer is high risk. - **Documentation**: Transfer Impact Assessment / DPIA, copy of the chosen SCCs (UK or EU), evidence of supplementary safeguards, updated processor agreement, records of processing activities, and employee consent where applicable. By following this checklist you’ll satisfy both UK and EU regimes, align with the latest enforcement trends, and keep your HR data transfer compliant.
